# Registered report: Discovery and preclinical validation of drug indications using compendia of public gene expression data ## Authors - Irawati Kandela1 - Ioannis Zervantonakis2 ### Affiliations 1. Developmental Therapeutics Core Northwestern University, Evanston Illinois United States 2. Harvard Medical School, Boston Massachusetts United States † Corresponding author ## Abstract The Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology seeks to address growing concerns about reproducibility in scientific research by conducting replications of 50 papers in the field of cancer biology published between 2010 and 2012. This Registered report describes the proposed replication plan of key experiments from ‘Discovery and Preclinical Validation of Drug Indications Using Compendia of Public Gene Expression Data’ by Sirota et al., published in Science Translational Medicine in 2011 (Sirota et al., 2011). The key experiments being replicated include Figure 4C and D and Supplemental Figure 1. In these figures, Sirota and colleagues. tested a proof of concept experiment validating their prediction that cimetidine, a histamine-2 (H2) receptor agonist commonly used to treat peptic ulcers (Kubecova et al., 2011), would be effective against lung adenocarcinoma (Figure 4C and D). As a control they also tested the effects of cimetidine against renal carcinoma, for which it was not predicted to be efficacious (Supplemental Figure 1). The Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology is a collaboration between the Center for Open Science and Science Exchange, and the results of the replications will be published by eLife. ## Introduction In this paper, Sirota and colleagues tested their hypothesis that extant drugs could be repurposed to target alternative diseases; if so, this could improve efficiency in the search for new treatments. They compared data from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO)—which they used to determine gene expression signatures of diseases—to data from the Connectivity Map, which tracks the changes in mRNA expression caused by 164 drugs. By comparing these two mRNA expression sets, Sirota and colleagues created a similarity score to describe how similar the changes in mRNA expression were between each drug and each disease. They theorized that a similarity score close to −1 (exactly opposite signatures) might indicate that the drug could treat the disease. In Figure 4C and D, Sirota and colleagues directly test their hypothesis by examining the effects of cimetidine, an H2 receptor blocker commonly used to treat gastric ulcers by reducing the production of stomach acid (Kubecova et al., 2011), on xenograft transplanted A549 lung adenocarcinoma cells. Mice treated with cimetidine showed a dose-dependent reduction in tumor size after 12 days of treatment. In Supplemental Figure 1, they also treated ACHN renal carcinoma cells with cimetidine, although cimetidine was not predicted to treat this cancer line. They observed no effect of cimetidine on the growth of this cancer cell line. These experiments will be replicated in Protocol 1. However, the conclusions that can be drawn from these experiments are limited by the fact that only a single cell line was tested with only a single drug. To date, no direct replication of the experiments presented in Sirota and colleagues' Figure 4C and D or Supplemental Figure 1 has been reported. However, Stoyanov and colleagues did examine the effect of cimetidine on growth of A459 cells activated with histamine and reported that cimetidine did reduce proliferation in vitro (Stoyanov et al., 2012). An exploratory analysis of a cohort of diabetic patients demonstrated a decreased risk of developing lung cancer, specifically adenocarcinoma, in patients who took over-the-counter H2 receptor blockers, including cimetidine (Hsu et al., 2013). ## Materials and methods Unless otherwise noted, all protocol information was derived from the original paper, references from the original paper, or information obtained directly from the authors. An asterisk (*) indicates data or information provided by the Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology core team. A hashtag (#) indicates information provided by the replicating lab. ### Protocol 1: assessing the effect of cimetidine treatment on tumor growth in a xenograft model of lung carcinoma and a xenograft model of renal carcinoma This protocol describes how to create xenograft tumors in severe combined immunodeficient (SCID) mice from A549 lung carcinoma cells (as seen in Figure 4C and D) or ACHN renal carcinoma cells (Supplemental Figure 1). Tumor growth is then assessed during 11 days of cimetidine treatment. Sirota and colleagues designed this experiment to test their predictions that A549 cells would be susceptible to cimetidine treatment while ACHN cells would not. Treatment with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) alone will serve as the negative control, while treatment with the lung adenocarcinoma standard drug doxorubicin will serve as the positive control. #### Sampling This experiment will use at least 12 mice per group for a final power of 82.4%.See ‘Power calculations’ for details.The experiment contains five cohorts total:A549 lung adenocarcinoma xenografts:a. Cohort 1: mice treated with PBS (negative control).i. N = 14.■ To ensure at least 12 tumors develop.b. Cohort 2: mice treated with 2 mg/kg doxorubicin (Dox) (positive control).i. N = 5.■ To ensure at least 3 tumors develop.c. Cohort 3: mice treated with 100 mg/kg cimetidine.i. N = 14.■ To ensure at least 12 tumors develop.ACHN renal carcinoma xenografts:a. Cohort 1: mice treated with PBS (negative control).i. N = 14.■ To ensure at least 12 tumors develop.b. Cohort 2: mice treated with 100 mg/kg cimetidine.i. N = 14.■ To ensure at least 12 tumors develop. #### Materials and reagents

#### Procedure Notes:A549 cells are maintained in F-12 Ham's medium supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS), 2 mM sodium pyruvate and 1 μM lipoic acid, based on ATCC recommendations.Lipoic acid is maintained as a 50 mg/ml stock in ethanol.ACHN cells are maintained in EMEM supplemented with 10% FBS, 2 mM glutamine and 1 mM sodium pyruvate, based on ATCC recommendations.All cells are grown at 37°C/5% CO2.All cell lines will be sent for STR profiling and mycoplasma testing.Culture A549 cells and ACHN cells.Resuspend 5 × 106 cells in 100# μl PBS per injection.Inject 5 × 106 cells (i.e., 100 µl of cell suspension) into the upper flank of 4–6-week-old* female SCID mice.a. Mice will be randomly assigned to receive injections with A549 cells or ACHN cells.i. Injections will be balanced so the total number of mice receiving A549 injections will be 33 and ACHN will be 28.Measure tumor volume with calipers daily.a. Record daily tumor volume.b. Volume is defined as mm3 = 0.52 × [width (cm)]2 × height (cm).i. Mice shall be euthanized if they appear in undue distress according to the replicating lab's guidelines; if the animal has lost >20% body weight.When tumor reaches a minimum of 100 mm3 in volume (estimated time 2–3 weeks#), initiate treatment. Continue treatment for 11 days past this point.a. As each mouse reaches the injection criteria (i.e., 100 mm3 tumor volume), randomly assign to a treatment group using the adaptive randomization approach with the time from injection of cells to when tumors reach at least 100 mm3 and tumor volume at time of assignment as the covariates that are assessed as mice are sequentially assigned to a particular treatment group.i. Assignment will also take into account the pre-determined size of each treatment group.b. Treat mice by intraperitoneal injection according to cohort:i. A459 lung adenocarcinoma xenografts:Cohort 1: PBS (daily).Cohort 2: 2 mg/kg Doxorubicin (biweekly).Cohort 3: 100 mg/kg cimetidine (daily).ii. ACHN renal carcinoma xenograft injections:Cohort 1: PBS (daily).Cohort 2: 100 mg/kg cimetidine (daily).c. Continue daily tumor volume measurements.Euthanize mice.a. Euthanize mice by CO2 inhalation followed by cervical dislocation.Harvest tumors and record weight (additional parameter).a. Image tumors alongside a ruler. #### Deliverables Data to be collected:Mouse health records, including age and tumor volume at start of injections, time of tumor detection, any excluded mice (including reason for exclusion).Raw data of tumor dimensions by day.Final weight of tumors.Graph of relative mean tumor weight in each cohort starting on Day 1 post-100 mm3 (as seen in Figure 4C and Supplemental Figure 1).a. Normalize Day 2 onwards to the weight at Day 1.Image of all tumors alongside ruler (as seen in Figure 4D) for both A459 xenografts and ACHN xenografts. #### Confirmatory analysis plan Statistical analysis of replication data:At the time of analysis, we will perform the Shapiro–Wilk test and generate a quantile–quantile (q–q) plot to attempt to assess the normality of the data and also perform Levene's test to assess homoscedasiticity. If the data appear skewed, we will attempt a transformation in order to proceed with the proposed statistical analysis listed below and possibly perform the appropriate non-parametric test.a. Comparison of the mean relative tumor weight of 100 mg/kg cimetidine treatment at day 11 as compared to PBS treatment at day 11 for both A549 and ACHN xenograft tumors.i. Two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) (2 × 2 factorial) followed by Bonferroni corrected Welch's t-tests for the following comparisons:■ PBS-treated A549 tumors vs cimetidine-treated A459 tumors.■ PBS-treated ACHN tumors vs cimetidine-treated ACHN tumors.ii. Additional comparison of PBS-treated A459 tumors to doxorubicin-treated tumors.■Bonferroni corrected Welch's t-test outside the framework of the ANOVA.Meta-analysis of original and replication attempt effect sizes:This replication attempt will perform the statistical analysis listed above, compute the effects sizes, compare them against the reported effect size in the original paper and use a meta-analytic approach to combine the original and replication effects, which will be presented as a forest plot. #### Known differences from the original study The replication attempt will encompass the PBS control, the doxorubicin control and the highest dose of cimetidine (100 mg/kg). It will not include the 25 mg/ml or 50 mg/ml cimetidine treatment groups.While the original study performed injections of 5 × 106 cells per microliter of PBS, on the advice of the replicating lab we will inject the same number of cells but suspended in 100 µl PBS. #### Provisions for quality control Mice will be randomly assigned to xenograft model and treatment type. All data obtained from the experiment—raw data, data analysis, control data and quality control data—will be made publicly available, either in the published manuscript or as an open access dataset available on the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/hxrmm/). ## Power calculations For details on power calculations, please see analysis files on the Open Science Framework:https://osf.io/uazfe/wiki/home/ ### Protocol 1 Note: data values estimated from published figures. # Peer review - Round 1

Editors:
- Chi Van Dang, University of Pennsylvania , United States

Reviewers:
- (Reviewers not individually listed)

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.06847.002](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.06847.002)

eLife posts the editorial decision letter and author response on a selection of the published articles (subject to the approval of the authors). An edited version of the letter sent to the authors after peer review is shown, indicating the substantive concerns or comments; minor concerns are not usually shown. Reviewers have the opportunity to discuss the decision before the letter is sent (see review process). Similarly, the author response typically shows only responses to the major concerns raised by the reviewers.

Thank you for sending your work entitled “Registered report: Discovery and preclinical validation of drug indications using compendia of public gene expression data” for consideration at eLife. Your article has been favorably evaluated by Stylianos Antonarakis (Senior editor), Chi Dang (Reviewing editor), and 3 reviewers, one of whom is a biostatistician.

The Reviewing editor and the reviewers discussed their comments before we reached this decision, and the Reviewing editor has assembled the following comments to help you prepare a revised submission.

In this study, the authors propose a study to reproduce the findings reported in Figure 4C/D and Supplementary Figure 1 from a previously published manuscript (Sirota et al. Sci Trans Med, 2010), which aimed at assessing the ability to predict drug repurposing opportunities based on connectivity map data analysis. Specifically, the previous Sci Trans Med paper reports that cimetidine, a histamine-2 (H2) receptor agonist commonly used to treat peptic ulcers, can diminish lung cancer tumorigenesis in vivo. There are several key concerns about the design of the study. The first concern is about the duration of the experiment and statistical analysis, and the second about conclusions drawn from using only one lung cancer cell line.

1) At the beginning of the Materials and methods section: The authors plan to follow the mice for 11 days instead of 12 days. Is there a good reason to follow the mice one day short? In addition, the experiment contains five cohorts. Among the five cohorts, cohort 2 only has 5 mice while the other 4 cohorts have 14 mice. Please justify.

2) Power calculation was based on t-test. It is suggested that the authors use two-tailed unequal variance t-test if normality is not violated or the use of Wilcoxon rank-sum test if normality is violated. The authors propose the use of two-way ANOVA followed by t-test for analyzing tumor weight data (in the subsection headed “Confirmatory analysis plan”). Please make sure that the data do not violate the assumptions of ANOVA: normality and homoscedasiticity. If the data do not fit the assumptions well enough, please try to find a data transformation that makes them fit. If this doesn't work, please apply a nonparametric counterpart of ANOVA such as Kruskal–Wallis test. In addition, I suggest the use of contrast within the ANOVA framework instead of t-test if the assumptions of ANOVA are met.

3) To compare growth curves of tumors, the authors propose ANCOVA followed by Bonferroni corrected t-test. Please make sure that the data do not violate the assumptions of ANCOVA and perform transformation or use non-parametric ANCOVA if needed.

4) For the additional comparison of PBS-treated A459 tumors to Doxorubicin treated tumors (in the subsection headed “Confirmatory analysis plan” and in the subsection headed “Test family”), I suggest the use of two-tailed unequal variance t-test instead of t-test if normality is not violated or the use of Wilcoxon rank-sum test if normality is violated.

5) Although the reproducibility project is aimed toward reproducing previously published results, the reviewers would like for the authors to address the limitation of drawing conclusions for the use of only one cell line, A549. Specifically, activity of drugs in cell lines and xenografts is generally highly idiosyncratic. As a result, most journals require that any in vitro and in vivo experiments are replicated in multiple cell lines and in vivo models.

results.result: This manuscript describes a registered replication report as part of the Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology, which aims to replicate 50 cancer biology papers published between 2010-2012. Specifically, this report details the planned replication of key experiments from Sirota et al. (2011) published in Science Translational Medicine.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C6, and C7 provide clear context about the project scope, the original study being replicated, and the collaborative framework. These are straightforward descriptive claims that are well-documented and verifiable.

results.result: Cimetidine is characterized as a histamine-2 (H2) receptor agonist/blocker commonly used to treat peptic/gastric ulcers.
results.evaluation: Claims C3 and C13 contain a critical pharmacological error. C3 describes cimetidine as an H2 receptor agonist, while C13 correctly identifies it as an H2 receptor blocker. Cimetidine is definitively an H2 receptor antagonist (blocker), not an agonist. This mischaracterization in C3 represents a fundamental error in describing the drug's mechanism of action.

results.result: The original Sirota et al. study hypothesized that drugs could be repurposed for alternative diseases by comparing gene expression signatures from GEO with drug-induced expression changes from the Connectivity Map. They predicted that cimetidine would be effective against lung adenocarcinoma but not renal carcinoma based on similarity scores.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C5, and C8-C12 accurately describe the original study's hypothesis, methodology, and predictions. The computational approach using GEO and Connectivity Map data to generate similarity scores is clearly explained, and the specific predictions about cimetidine's efficacy are well-documented from the original paper.

results.result: The original study found that cimetidine treatment resulted in dose-dependent tumor reduction in A549 lung adenocarcinoma xenografts after 12 days, but had no effect on ACHN renal carcinoma xenografts. However, these conclusions are limited by testing only a single cell line with a single drug.
results.evaluation: Claims C14, C15, and C16 accurately summarize the original findings and appropriately acknowledge the limitation of single cell line testing. The critical assessment in C16 is reasonable and important for contextualizing the scope of the original conclusions.

results.result: No direct replication of the original Sirota experiments has been reported, though related studies provide supporting evidence: Stoyanov et al. showed cimetidine reduced A549 proliferation in vitro, and Hsu et al. found decreased lung adenocarcinoma risk in diabetic patients taking H2 blockers including cimetidine.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C19 provide appropriate context about the replication status and related supporting literature. The distinction between direct replication and related studies is clearly made, and the supporting evidence is appropriately characterized as exploratory or in vitro.

results.result: The replication study is designed with 12 mice per group to achieve 82.4-84.36% statistical power, with 33 total mice receiving A549 injections and 28 receiving ACHN injections. Power calculations used the PBS control group SD as the divisor.
results.evaluation: Claims C20, C51, C52, C56, and C57 provide consistent information about sample size planning and power calculations. The power analysis appears appropriately designed with adequate justification for the chosen sample sizes, though the slight discrepancy between 82.4% and 84.36% power estimates should be clarified.

results.result: Cell culture conditions are specified following ATCC recommendations: A549 cells in F-12 Ham's medium with supplements, ACHN cells in EMEM with supplements, both at 37°C/5% CO2. Quality control includes STR profiling and mycoplasma testing.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C23, C48, and C50 provide detailed, standard cell culture protocols with appropriate quality control measures. The inclusion of STR profiling and mycoplasma testing represents good experimental practice for ensuring cell line authenticity and sterility.

results.result: The xenograft protocol involves injecting 5×10^6 cells into SCID mice, measuring tumor volume daily with calipers using a specified formula, initiating treatment when tumors reach 100 mm³, and continuing for 11 days. Adaptive randomization will be used with time to tumor development and initial tumor volume as covariates.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C28 and C63 describe a well-designed xenograft protocol with appropriate randomization strategy. The adaptive randomization approach accounting for relevant covariates is methodologically sound and should help control for variability in tumor development.

results.result: Treatment groups include PBS control (daily), doxorubicin positive control (2 mg/kg biweekly for A549 only), and cimetidine (100 mg/kg daily for both cell lines). Humane endpoints include euthanasia by CO2/cervical dislocation if mice show distress or >20% weight loss.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C31 and C49 specify appropriate treatment regimens and humane endpoints. The inclusion of both negative (PBS) and positive (doxorubicin) controls for A549 xenografts is methodologically sound, and the humane endpoints are standard and ethical.

results.result: The replication differs from the original study by excluding the 25 mg/kg and 50 mg/kg cimetidine doses and by injecting cells in 100 µl PBS rather than per microliter of PBS.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C34 transparently document known differences from the original protocol. The modification to injection volume (100 µl total) based on replicating lab advice is reasonable and well-justified, though C33's description of the original protocol as '5×10^6 cells per microliter' appears to be a misinterpretation.

results.result: Statistical analysis will include two-way ANOVA (2×2 factorial) followed by Bonferroni-corrected Welch's t-tests, with preliminary assessment of normality (Shapiro-Wilk test, Q-Q plots) and homoscedasticity (Levene's test). A meta-analytic approach will combine original and replication effect sizes in a forest plot.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C47 describe an appropriate and comprehensive statistical analysis plan. The inclusion of normality and homoscedasticity testing, the use of Welch's t-tests (which don't assume equal variances), and the planned meta-analysis demonstrate statistical rigor. The contingency for non-parametric tests if assumptions are violated is appropriate.

results.result: Power calculations were based on data values estimated from published figures, with error bars assumed to represent SEM, and standard deviation calculated using SD = SEM*(SQRT n).
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C55 reveal that power calculations rely on estimated data extracted from figures and an assumption about error bar representation. While the mathematical conversion from SEM to SD (C55) is correct, the reliance on figure extraction (C53) and assumption about error bars (C54) introduces uncertainty. The original paper should have been consulted to verify whether error bars represent SEM or SD, as this assumption directly affects power calculations.

results.result: Data collection and sharing procedures include making all raw data, analysis, and quality control data publicly available on the Open Science Framework, imaging tumors with rulers, recording final tumor weights, and normalizing tumor weights to Day 1 values.
results.evaluation: Claims C35, C64-C66 describe appropriate data management, collection, and transparency practices. The commitment to open data sharing and the inclusion of multiple measurement modalities (volume, weight, imaging) strengthen the replication's rigor and reproducibility.

results.result: The replication study plans to follow mice for 11 days of treatment after tumors reach 100 mm³, which is one day shorter than the 12 days reported in the original study.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly questioned this discrepancy, asking 'Is there a good reason to follow the mice one day short?' This indicates concern about the deviation from the original protocol without clear justification provided in the manuscript.

results.result: The experimental design allocates different numbers of mice across cohorts, with 33 mice receiving A549 injections and 28 receiving ACHN injections, resulting in unequal cohort sizes (cohort 2 has 5 mice while other cohorts have 14 mice).
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly requested justification for the unequal allocation, stating 'cohort 2 only has 5 mice while the other 4 cohorts have 14 mice. Please justify.' This indicates the reviewers found the sample size distribution unclear or potentially problematic.

results.result: The statistical analysis plan includes two-way ANOVA followed by Bonferroni corrected Welch's t-tests, with normality assessed by Shapiro-Wilk test and quantile-quantile plots, and homoscedasticity assessed by Levene's test.
results.evaluation: Reviewers raised multiple concerns about the statistical approach, requesting that authors 'make sure that the data do not violate the assumptions of ANOVA: normality and homoscedasiticity' and suggesting alternative approaches including data transformation or non-parametric tests (Kruskal-Wallis) if assumptions are violated. They also suggested using contrasts within ANOVA framework instead of t-tests. This indicates the statistical plan requires conditional modifications based on data properties.

results.result: Power calculations were performed using R software and G*Power, determining that 12 mice per group would provide 82.4-84.36% power, with calculations based on t-test and using PBS control group SD as the divisor.
results.evaluation: Reviewers noted that 'Power calculation was based on t-test' and suggested the authors should use 'two-tailed unequal variance t-test if normality is not violated or the use of Wilcoxon rank-sum test if normality is violated.' This indicates concern that the power calculation method may not align with the appropriate statistical test for the actual data.

results.result: The original study by Sirota et al. showed that cimetidine produced dose-dependent reduction in A549 lung adenocarcinoma tumor size but had no effect on ACHN renal carcinoma, though conclusions are limited by testing only a single cell line with a single drug.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly raised concern about the limitation of using only one cell line (A549), stating 'the reviewers would like for the authors to address the limitation of drawing conclusions for the use of only one cell line' and noting that 'activity of drugs in cell lines and xenografts is generally highly idiosyncratic' and 'most journals require that any in vitro and in vivo experiments are replicated in multiple cell lines and in vivo models.' This indicates the reviewers view the single cell line approach as a significant limitation.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluate claims C14, C15, and C16 regarding the original study's findings and the limitation of single cell line testing. OpenEval finds these claims SUPPORTED and views the critical assessment as reasonable, while peer reviewers mark them UNCERTAIN and explicitly request the authors address this limitation, noting that most journals require multiple cell lines. This represents a disagreement in severity: OpenEval accepts the acknowledgment of limitation as sufficient, while reviewers see it as a significant methodological concern requiring justification.

Both address statistical analysis claims C44, C45, and C46. OpenEval finds the statistical plan SUPPORTED, noting the appropriateness of normality/homoscedasticity testing and contingency for non-parametric tests. Peer reviewers mark this UNCERTAIN and request explicit verification that assumptions are not violated, suggest data transformation or Kruskal-Wallis tests if needed, and recommend using contrasts within ANOVA instead of t-tests. While both acknowledge the conditional nature of the analysis, reviewers require more explicit methodological justification.

Both evaluate power calculation claims (C20, C56, C57 overlap, plus C43 in peer review). OpenEval finds the power analysis SUPPORTED with appropriate justification. Peer reviewers mark it UNCERTAIN, noting the power calculation was based on t-test and suggesting alignment with the appropriate statistical test (two-tailed unequal variance t-test or Wilcoxon rank-sum test depending on normality). This represents concern about consistency between power calculation assumptions and actual statistical methods.

Both address sample size claims C51 and C52. OpenEval finds these SUPPORTED, noting the power analysis appears appropriately designed with adequate justification. Peer reviewers mark them UNCERTAIN and explicitly request justification for the unequal allocation (cohort 2 with 5 mice versus other cohorts with 14 mice). OpenEval did not identify this specific concern about unequal distribution across cohorts.

Both evaluate claim C27 regarding the xenograft protocol timeline. OpenEval finds the overall xenograft protocol (C24-C28, C63) SUPPORTED with appropriate randomization. Peer reviewers specifically question C27 UNCERTAIN, asking 'Is there a good reason to follow the mice one day short?' indicating concern about the 28-day versus 29-day deviation from the original protocol. OpenEval did not flag this specific timeline discrepancy as problematic.

OpenEval found claims C1, C2, C6, and C7 (project scope, original study context, collaborative framework) SUPPORTED as straightforward descriptive claims. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these contextual claims.

OpenEval identified a critical pharmacological error in claims C3 and C13, marking them UNSUPPORTED due to C3 incorrectly describing cimetidine as an H2 receptor agonist when it is definitively an antagonist. No corresponding peer review evaluation found addressing this fundamental error.

OpenEval found claims C4, C5, C8-C12 (original study's hypothesis, methodology, computational approach, and predictions) SUPPORTED as accurately describing the original paper. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these methodological description claims.

OpenEval found claims C17-C19 (replication status and supporting literature context) SUPPORTED, noting appropriate distinction between direct replication and related studies. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these contextual claims.

OpenEval found claims C21-C23, C48, and C50 (cell culture protocols and quality control) SUPPORTED as detailed standard protocols with appropriate STR profiling and mycoplasma testing. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these technical protocol claims.

OpenEval found claims C29-C31 and C49 (treatment regimens, controls, and humane endpoints) SUPPORTED as methodologically sound with appropriate negative and positive controls. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these treatment protocol claims.

OpenEval found claims C32-C34 (known protocol differences) SUPPORTED, noting transparent documentation of modifications with reasonable justification, though identifying a potential misinterpretation in C33. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these protocol deviation claims.

OpenEval marked claims C53-C55 UNCERTAIN due to power calculations relying on estimated data extracted from figures and assumptions about error bar representation (SEM vs SD). While the mathematical conversion is correct, the reliance on figure extraction introduces uncertainty. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing this data extraction concern.

OpenEval found claims C35, C64-C66 (data management, collection, transparency practices, and open data sharing) SUPPORTED as appropriate practices strengthening rigor and reproducibility. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these data management claims.
